question: The most popular paradigm of mental health consultation has been proposed by
options: Satir and Minuchin.
Schein.
Caplan.
Bandura.
rationale: Mental health consultation occurs when a consultant works with a consultee regarding clients or administrative/program issues. When the ultimate goal is to help a client, it is known as a “clientcentered” consultation. When your licensing supervisor suggests a plan of action for a given client, then you as a consultee are the recipient of “client-centered” consultation (not to be confused with clientcentered therapy). The exam you will take also may mention “consultee-centered” consultation. Here, the focus is on helping the consultee develop improved techniques or skills. Thus, when your licensing supervisor explains a better way for you to implement a hypnotic induction with one of your clients, then you are the recipient of “consultee-centered case consultation.” A variation of this is the “consultee-centered administrative consultation” in which your supervisor’s or consultant’s intention is to sharpen up your administrative skills (e.g., making you a better presenter at your agency board meeting). Finally, there is the “program-centered administrative consultation.” As the name suggests, the emphasis here is on creating, designing, or evaluating the program in question. These four basic types of mental health consultation have been proposed by Gerald Caplan. Choice “a” identifies two well-known names in the family therapy movement, while Albert Bandura (choice “d”) is well-known for his work in modeling and vicarious learning by observation (sometimes known as “social learning theory”). In this approach, the consultant helps the consultee set up behavioral management programs for the clients.

question: The doctor–patient consultation model relies on four distinct stages: entry, diagnosis, implementation, and evaluation. In order for the doctor–patient structure to work, the consultee (i.e., the person receiving the consultation) must accurately depict symptomatology, trust the consultant’s diagnosis, and carry out the consultant’s directives. This model is associated most closely with the work of
options: Caplan.
Freud.
Adler.
Schein.
rationale: Consultants can focus on process (what is happening from a communications standpoint) or content (knowledge imparted from the consultant to the consultee).

question: ________ are the leading causes of malpractice actions taken against counselors, therapists, and mental health providers.
options: Confidentiality and dual relationships
Termination
Failure of the duty to warn
Inferior record keeping
rationale: Sexual issues also make it into the top ten slots and indeed I have even seen research that puts it in the number one spot. It has been estimated that over 95% of those clients who were sexually involved with their therapists have been harmed, and that in about one third of the cases, treatment literally ended as soon as sexual intimacy began. Important reminder many counselors are not aware of: Excessive selfdisclosure on the part of the helper can be considered malpractice. If it doesn’t help the client and is seemingly intended to help the counselor then it is inappropriate.

question: Your client was seeing Dr. Doyle for counseling for three years. The client has now stopped seeing Dr. Doyle and has an appointment to see you. You should
options: refuse to see the client unless she will sign a release so you can secure the information Dr. Doyle compiled.
call Dr. Doyle. In this situation no release of information or consent form is necessary.
counsel the client.
put something in writing and send it to Dr. Doyle prior to the second session of counseling.
rationale: Treat this client in the same manner as you would treat any other client! To be sure, you might decide that information amassed via Dr. Doyle would be helpful and then you would secure the client’s written permission to contact him. Nevertheless, this certainly isn’t required to begin the counseling process. Moreover, it is possible that the client will not sign for the release.

question: You are treating a man who suffers from panic disorder. His panic attacks are so severe he cannot drive to work. After just three sessions he is not only driving to work but has taken up sky diving to demonstrate his progress over his fear. You would love to put his testimonial on your brochure to show how adept you are at treating this affliction. You should
options: ask him if he will write you a few sentences to place on the brochure with his name at the end.
ask him if you can write the testimonial for him and place it on the brochure.
not ask him for a testimonial since it would constitute an ethics violation.
ask him if he will write you a few sentences to place on the brochure but assure him that his name will not appear.
rationale: Ethics guidelines clearly state that the counselor should not solicit testimonials from clients.

question: Ethical dilemmas rarely have clear-cut answers. Thus when a complex ethical situation manifests itself, it is best to
options: consult only ethical codes and not colleagues.
consult with colleagues as well as ethical codes inasmuch as legal standards are very often based on the methods of fellow professionals in analogous situations.
consult ACA but not your colleagues.
consult your state licensing bureau but not your colleagues.
rationale: Legal standards and cases regarding malpractice suits are often decided by the behavior of your fellow professionals. If I were you, I’d check to make certain you’re not the one soldier marching in the opposite direction! In malpractice cases you are often judged by what your peers would do in the situation.

question: You have attempted to help a client for over two years with little or no success. You should
options: always refer the client to a board-certified psychiatrist.
terminate the relationship and initiate an appropriate referral.
change therapeutic modalities and see the client for another six months.
change therapeutic modalities and see the client for at least another year.
rationale: Ethics guidelines suggest that when a counselor feels he or she is unable to help a potential or existing client, then the relationship should not be initiated, or the existing one should be terminated. In either case, the counselor is responsible for providing alternative referral sources to the client.

question: Assume that you have decided to refer a client elsewhere because you were unable to help her. Upon you mentioning this, the client insists that she has seen several other therapists and you are the finest one. Ethics guidelines would dictate that
options: you must see her; your duty is to the client.
you must refer her to a medical practitioner.
you must ask her to consider hospitalization.
you are not obligated to continue the relationship.
rationale: You are acting in the best interest of the client.

question: Counseling is a relatively new profession. The first counselors in the United States were not called counselors. They were
options: psychoanalysts practicing short-term therapy.
behaviorists practicing short-term therapy.
deans and advisors employed after the Civil War in college settings to watch over young women.
humanistic psychologists.

question: Historically speaking, the first psychology laboratory was set up by
options: Frank Parsons, who set up community centers to help individuals in search of work.
Sigmund Freud, the father of psychoanalysis.
Wilhelm Wundt, in 1879 in Leipzig, Germany.
E. G. Williamson.
rationale: Wundt was convinced that psychology could be accepted as a science if consciousness could be measured. Wundt’s school of thought is termed structuralism because his interest was in the “structure” of consciousness. German psychologists—and I’m certain you’ll find this humorous in terms of our emphasis today on pragmatic strategies—were convinced that Wundt’s theory was indeed pure science because it had no practical applications! Parsons, choice “a,” has been called the father of guidance. Some historians insist that the profession of counseling officially began when Parsons founded the Vocational Guidance Bureau of Boston and published the book Choosing a Vocation in 1909.

question: Counseling became popular after the 1931 publication of
options: Workbook in Vocations by William Proctor, Glidden Ross Benefield, and Gilbert Wrenn.
The Interpretation of Dreams by Sigmund Freud.
Behaviorism by John B.Watson. (c)
Counseling and Psychotherapy by Carl Ransom Rogers.
rationale: These are all landmark books in the field. Choice “a” is the correct answer because it set the stage for the popularization of the word counseling. Prior to 1931, the word guidance was used for educational and vocational guidance. This work, as well as an earlier one by William Proctor in 1925 entitled Educational and Vocational Guidance, began to conceptualize counseling as a psychological process. Choice “b” is considered Freud’s most influential work, while choice “c” described the tenets of behaviorism, which was born in 1912. Watson’s behaviorism asserted that the only subject matter for psychology was observable behavior. Choice “d” is the 1942 classic in which Rogers emphasized a theory of intervention in which the counselor was not an authoritarian figure such as in psychoanalysis, trait-factor analysis, or directive schools of helping. Rogers was also known as one of the first theorists to employ audio recordings to improve practicum supervision.

question: PL 94-142 (the Education for All Handicapped Children Act) states that
options: all children between ages 5 and 21 are assured free education.
handicapped persons are placed in the least-restrictive environment (LRE).
an Individualized Education Plan (IEP) is developed for each child
all of the above.
rationale: Note: The term disabled is now preferred over the antiquated term handicapped. The Act was passed in 1975—a year before Virginia passed the first counselor licensure law—after a congressional finding that the United States had over eight million children who were disabled. Over half were not receiving appropriate education while one million were excluded from public education. Enforcement relied on funding. That is to say, if a state did not meet the guidelines mentioned in choices “a,” “b,” and “c,” funding was denied. Section 617 (c) of PL 94-142 (another stipulation for funding) gave individuals the right to read their own records and files if they were over 18, as well as the records of their children. In 1990, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) prohibited employers with 15 or more employees from discriminating against the disabled.

question: The major trend that impacted upon the counseling movement in the 1980s
options: was reality therapy.
was behavior modification.
included an emphasis on professionalism, certification, and licensing.
was the group movement.
rationale: Credentialing helped counseling become a specific and separate profession such as psychology or psychiatry. Although group work is still very popular, it emerged as a driving force in the 1970s.

question: The APGA and APA had joint ethics guidelines for counselors and psychologists. This changed during the 1970s when 384
options: Psy.D. programs were introduced.
the APA did not wish to credential master’s level counselors or psychologists.
psychologists were doing more testing.
joint ethics became illegal in the United States.
rationale: Separate ethics were thus developed, which helped discern counseling from psychology as a profession. Psy.D., or doctor of psychology programs (choice “a”), generally focus more on practitioner skills and less on research and experimental skills than Ph.D. programs in clinical psychology.

question: The 1950s was the age of tremendous strides in
options: analysis.
developmental psychology.
behavior modification.
group work.
rationale: Piaget, Erikson, and Havinghurst were very influential. In addition, thanks primarily to the work of Carl R. Rogers, counseling rather than testing became the major task for professionals.

question: The ________ movement began in the late 1960s.
options: testing
Rogerian
group
developmental psychology
rationale: Groups would remain popular in the 1970s. Some of the literature in the field refers to the 1960s and 1970s as “decades of variation,” in which we became “therapy of the month consumers”! Jerome Frank hypothesized at the time that the sudden flood of new therapies was due to the current upheaval in society. Gestalt, transactional analysis, primal scream therapy, encounter groups, marathon groups, and yes, even naked encounter groups became popular!

question: In the 1960s C. Gilbert Wrenn’s book, The Counselor in a Changing World, urged counselors to
options: use biofeedback.
rely more heavily on projective testing.
emphasize developmental concerns rather than merely focusing on crises and curing emotional illness.
stick to proven nondirective techniques.
rationale: This 1962 APGA publication was an attempt to steer counseling away from merely providing remedial services to students.

question: One of the primary problems of counseling in the early 1960s was that it wrongly emphasized 385
options: social issues.
intrapsychic processes.
referrals to secure antidepressant medicine.
career counseling.
rationale: Choice “b” is correct, intrapsychic processes (i.e., processes within one’s mind or psyche). This was not entirely a negative thing; nevertheless, social issues such as Vietnam, civil rights, and women’s issues could have been emphasized to a greater degree.

question: The significance of the 1958 National Defense Education Act was that it
options: provided financial aid for graduate education in counseling.
expanded school guidance services.
improved guidance for gifted children.
all of the above.
rationale: Many pilot programs developed as a result of the funding. Gradually, the funding found its way into helping counselors prepare to work with economically disadvantaged youth. Thus, the Act eventually helped all types of young people secure better counseling and guidance services. Some exams may use the abbreviation NDEA when referring to this act.

question: A man has a rare, highly contagious disease that is fatal. He is keeping it a secret and insists that he will never tell his wife. You should
options: break confidentiality and tell his wife.
honor the man’s decision not to tell his wife for therapeutic reasons.
honor the man’s decision not to tell his wife in order to maintain ethical confidentiality.
handle it based on your clinical intuition since ethical guidelines fail to address this emotionally charged issue.
rationale: Ethics tell us that if a client has a contagious fatal disease the counselor is justified in telling a third party who would be at serious and foreseeable risk. Of course, the counselor must ascertain that the client has not already informed this person or that the client does not intend to inform the third party in a reasonable period of time.
